120.title: Ramadan: the new moon
120.hook: the month begins when the crescent is seen or the month is counted
120.howItsDone: Muslims begin and end Ramadan by the new crescent moon: some communities wait for a local sighting, some follow a sighting elsewhere, and some use astronomical calculation, so start dates can differ by a day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: salawat, blessings on the Prophet, one sent and ten returned. Your line was peace on him. Did you catch the little symbol, and read it? Day one hundred twenty.

It's the evening after the twenty-ninth day of the month before Ramadan. Just after sunset, on a hill outside a city, a small group of people stand facing west with binoculars, squinting at the sky where the sun just went down. In a family group chat, someone keeps asking: is it tomorrow? Has anyone seen it? Somewhere else, a committee is on the phone with people in three countries. Everyone's looking for the same thing: a thread of light, thinner than a fingernail clipping, low in the sky for a few minutes before it sets. Today: the new moon.
screen: `FACING WEST AFTER SUNSET.` → `IS IT TOMORROW?` → `A THREAD OF LIGHT.`

segments.voice: That thread of light is the hilal, the crescent: the first sliver of the new moon. The Islamic calendar is lunar. Each month begins with the hilal and lasts twenty-nine or thirty days. That's why Ramadan moves about eleven days earlier every year, as you heard on day eighteen. The Qur'an, in Surah al-Baqarah, says people ask about the new moons, and answers that they are markers of time for people, and for the pilgrimage. So the sky is the calendar. A hadith in Bukhari gives the rule: fast when you see it, and stop fasting when you see it. And if it's hidden from you by clouds, complete the month as thirty days. Simple on a clear night in Medina. Harder for two billion people in every time zone. So Muslims today follow different approaches, and they're open about it. Some communities wait for a local sighting, with their own eyes, where they live. Some follow a sighting anywhere in the world, or in a particular country, often Saudi Arabia. Some, including major councils in North America and Europe, use astronomical calculation to fix the dates ahead of time. That's why two mosques in the same city sometimes start Ramadan a day apart, and why the group chat is so busy. There's also a short prayer from the Prophet ﷺ for the moment the crescent is seen, reported in Tirmidhi: asking that the month come with blessing, faith, safety and peace, and ending, speaking to the moon itself: my Lord and your Lord is Allah.
screen: `HILAL — THE FIRST SLIVER.` · `MARKERS OF TIME FOR PEOPLE.` · `FAST WHEN YOU SEE IT.` · `SIGHTING, OR COUNTING.` · then, large: `MY LORD AND YOUR LORD IS ALLAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for the moon tonight. If you can, step outside, or to a window, after dark, and find it. Notice its shape: a sliver, a half, a full circle, or not there at all. Wherever it is in its month, it's counting days for someone. If it's too early, close your eyes now and picture that thin crescent low in the west just after sunset. Breathe slowly. If you pray, you can say the Prophet's words to it: my Lord and your Lord is Allah. The bell holds the time.
Hilal. The crescent of the new moon, the first sliver that begins every Islamic month, and Ramadan. Today's word.
Your line: watch for the crescent. Look up at the moon once tonight or tomorrow, and see where it is in its month. Whenever Ramadan comes for you, this is how it starts. Day one hundred twenty.

121.title: Ramadan: the early meal
121.hook: eat before dawn, for there is blessing in it (Bukhari)
121.howItsDone: During Ramadan, Muslims who fast wake before dawn to eat suhur, often dates, water and simple food, and stop eating and drinking at the start of dawn, when the time of fajr begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday: hilal, the crescent of the new moon. Your line was watch for the crescent. Did you look up and find the moon in its month? Day one hundred twenty-one.

It's three forty-five in the morning. In old neighborhoods of Cairo or Istanbul, during Ramadan, a man may still walk the dark streets beating a small drum and calling out names, waking people up. In a suburban kitchen, a phone alarm goes off, and someone stumbles in, eyes half shut, and starts the kettle. Oats. Dates. Eggs. A lot of water. Nobody's hungry at this hour. Everyone's eating anyway. There's a reason for it, and the Prophet ﷺ gave it in one line. Today: the early meal.
screen: `THREE FORTY-FIVE IN THE MORNING.` → `A DRUM IN THE DARK STREETS.` → `NOBODY'S HUNGRY. EVERYONE EATS.`

segments.voice: The meal is called suhur, from sahar, the last part of the night, just before dawn. The line is in Bukhari: take the suhur meal, for in suhur there is blessing. Barakah. That word means more than a benefit. It's a kind of quiet abundance, when a little turns out to be enough. And the practical side is obvious: a long day without food or water goes better if you start it fed. But how do you know when to stop? The Qur'an, in Surah al-Baqarah, says eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of the dawn. And there's a lovely story about that verse, also in Bukhari. A companion named Adi ibn Hatim took it literally. He put a white thread and a black thread under his pillow, and all night he kept looking at them, waiting to tell them apart. He couldn't. In the morning he told the Prophet, who, in one telling, teased him that his pillow must be very wide, and explained: it means the darkness of the night and the whiteness of the day. The white thread is the first line of light along the horizon. Another companion, Zayd ibn Thabit, said they ate suhur with the Prophet and then stood for the prayer, and when asked how long between them, said: about as long as reciting fifty verses. So the meal was late, close to dawn. Not a midnight snack. A small, deliberate meal in the dark, eaten on purpose, as the last thing before the day's long quiet.
screen: `SUHUR — FROM SAHAR, BEFORE DAWN.` · `IN SUHUR THERE IS BLESSING.` · `A WHITE THREAD AND A BLACK THREAD.` · `ABOUT FIFTY VERSES BEFORE THE PRAYER.` · then, large: `A SMALL MEAL, IN THE DARK, ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan tomorrow's water before dawn. Picture tomorrow morning, a little earlier than you usually wake. Where's the glass? Where will you sit? Picture drinking it slowly, in the dark, before the day starts asking things of you. If you fast, plan your suhur the same way: simple, late, on purpose. If you don't, just decide on one glass of water before anything else tomorrow, and say to yourself: blessing before dawn. The bell holds the time.
Suhur. The meal before dawn in Ramadan, eaten late, for in it there is blessing. Today's word.
Your line: blessing before dawn. Tomorrow, let the first thing into your body be a glass of water, taken slowly, before the phone. Day one hundred twenty-one.

122.title: Ramadan: breaking with a date
122.hook: at sunset, a date and water, and a du'a
122.howItsDone: At sunset during Ramadan, Muslims break the fast promptly, often with dates and water, pray maghrib, and then eat the evening meal, frequently at communal iftars in mosques and homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: suhur, the meal before dawn, and the two threads. Your line was blessing before dawn. Was a glass of water the first thing into your day? Day one hundred twenty-two.

A long table in a mosque hall, paper cloths, plastic cups. A hundred people sitting down, some who know each other, some who don't: a student far from home, a taxi driver on his break, an elderly couple, a neighbor who isn't Muslim but was invited. Nobody's eating. Every plate has a few dates on it, and a cup of water. Everyone's watching the clock, or listening. Then, from the front, the call to the sunset prayer begins, and a hundred hands reach, at the same moment, for one small date. Today: breaking the fast.
screen: `A LONG TABLE, A HUNDRED PEOPLE.` → `A FEW DATES ON EVERY PLATE.` → `A HUNDRED HANDS, ONE MOMENT.`

segments.voice: It's called iftar, from a root that means to break open, to split. It's the meal that breaks the fast, at sunset, as maghrib comes in. And the way it starts goes back to the Prophet ﷺ. A companion, Anas, said the Prophet would break his fast with fresh dates before praying. If there were none, with dried dates. If there were none, with a few sips of water. That's all. Not a feast first. Something small and sweet, and water. The feast, if there is one, comes after. And there's a hurry to it, a good one. A hadith in Bukhari says people will remain in good as long as they hasten to break the fast. Don't linger to prove how strong you are. When the sun's gone, eat. There's a short prayer reported for the moment, too, in the Sunan of Abu Dawud: the thirst has gone, the veins are moistened, and the reward is confirmed, if Allah wills. Three plain facts, said with a date still in your mouth. Then the line that makes the moment sweet. In Bukhari, the Prophet said the fasting person has two joys: one when they break their fast, and one when they meet their Lord. The first joy is right there at the table. And the tradition asks you to share it. A hadith in Tirmidhi says whoever gives food to a fasting person to break their fast has the same reward as the one who fasted, without taking anything away from theirs. That's why mosques set out those long tables, and why so many people are invited.
screen: `IFTAR — TO BREAK OPEN.` · `FRESH DATES, DRIED DATES, OR WATER.` · `HASTEN TO BREAK THE FAST.` · `TWO JOYS.` · then, large: `FEED ONE, SHARE THE REWARD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: break one fast gently. It doesn't have to be a day's fast. It can be the few hours since you last ate. Before your next meal, take something small and sweet first, a date if you have one, or a piece of fruit, and a glass of water. Sit down for it. Eat it slowly. Notice the first taste of sweetness, and the water going down. Then wait a moment before the rest. If you pray, you can say bismillah first. The bell holds the time.
Iftar. The meal that breaks the fast at sunset: a date, water, a few words, and the first of two joys. Today's word.
Your line: sweet at sunset. Tonight, start your evening meal with something small and sweet, and if you can, share it with someone. Day one hundred twenty-two.

123.title: Ramadan: the night prayers
123.hook: long night prayers in the mosque, the whole Qur'an recited over the month
123.howItsDone: During Ramadan, many Sunni Muslims gather after the night prayer for tarawih, eight or twenty rak'ahs led by a reciter who often completes the whole Qur'an over the month; many Shia Muslims pray extra Ramadan night prayers individually.

segments.voice: Yesterday: iftar, breaking the fast with a date and water, the first of two joys. Your line was sweet at sunset. Did you start your evening with something small and sweet? Day one hundred twenty-three.

Ten at night in Ramadan, and the mosque parking lot is fuller than on a Friday. Inside, rows and rows of people, shoulder to shoulder, standing. At the front, one voice is reciting, and it keeps going, page after page, clear and long. Kids fall asleep on the carpet at the back. A grandmother sits on a chair by the wall. The standing lasts an hour, sometimes more. And by the last night of the month, if you'd come every night, you'd have heard the whole Qur'an, cover to cover. Today: the night prayers.
screen: `TEN AT NIGHT, A FULL PARKING LOT.` → `ONE VOICE, PAGE AFTER PAGE.` → `COVER TO COVER BY MONTH'S END.`

segments.voice: These prayers are called tarawih, from a word for rest, because the people who prayed them long ago would sit and rest after every four units. The prayer is voluntary, not one of the five, but in Ramadan it has a special place. A hadith in Bukhari says: whoever stands in prayer in Ramadan out of faith and hoping for reward, their past sins are forgiven. And here's the story of how it began. Aisha said that one Ramadan the Prophet ﷺ prayed at night in the mosque, and some people prayed behind him. The next night more came. The next, more still. Then one night, the mosque was full, and he didn't come out. In the morning he explained: I saw what you were doing, and nothing kept me away except that I feared it would be made obligatory on you. He didn't want to turn a gift into a burden. Years later, the second caliph, Umar, walked into the mosque one Ramadan night and found people praying in scattered little groups, each behind a different reciter. So he gathered them behind one reciter, a companion named Ubayy ibn Ka'b. And the next night, seeing them all together, he said: what a fine new thing this is. How many units? Communities differ, openly. Some pray eight, following a report from Aisha. Many pray twenty, as in the great mosque in Mecca. Many Shia Muslims pray the extra night prayers of Ramadan on their own, not in congregation. But everywhere, the idea is the same. The days of Ramadan are for fasting. The nights are for standing.
screen: `TARAWIH — FROM A WORD FOR REST.` · `STAND IN RAMADAN, OUT OF FAITH.` · `HE FEARED IT WOULD BE MADE A DUTY.` · `UMAR GATHERED THEM BEHIND ONE.` · then, large: `EIGHT, OR TWENTY, OR ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand a little longer tonight. Before bed, stand still for a minute or two, feet planted, hands folded or at your sides. If you pray, add two voluntary rak'ahs tonight, or make one standing a little longer than usual, reciting slowly. If you don't, just stand in a quiet room, and listen to the house at night. Notice how different the night feels from the day. When your legs start to ask to sit, stay one breath longer. The bell holds the time.
Tarawih. The long night prayers of Ramadan, named for the rests between them, the Qur'an recited over the month. Today's word.
Your line: the nights are for standing. Tonight, give the last ten minutes before sleep to something quiet, instead of a screen. Day one hundred twenty-three.

124.title: Ramadan: the Night of Power
124.hook: a night better than a thousand months, sought in the last ten (97:1–5)
124.tomorrow: Ramadan: the fast of the tongue
124.howItsDone: In the last ten nights of Ramadan, Muslims seek Laylat al-Qadr with extra prayer, Qur'an recitation and supplication, especially on the odd nights and often the twenty-seventh, and some stay in the mosque in retreat (i'tikaf).

segments.voice: Yesterday: tarawih, the long night prayers, named for their rests. Your line was the nights are for standing. Did you give the last minutes before sleep to something quiet? Day one hundred twenty-four.

A thousand months is about eighty-three years. A whole lifetime, most of one anyway. Now imagine being told that somewhere in the next ten nights there's one night worth more than all of that. You're not told which one. You're told it's one of them, probably an odd one. What would you do? Most people would do exactly what Muslims do in the last ten nights of Ramadan: stay up, show up, and try not to miss it. Mosques stay full past midnight. Some people don't go home at all. Today: the Night of Power.
screen: `A THOUSAND MONTHS: A LIFETIME.` → `ONE NIGHT WORTH MORE.` → `YOU'RE NOT TOLD WHICH.`

segments.voice: It's called Laylat al-Qadr. Laylah is night. Qadr is harder to translate: power, measure, decree, worth. Pickthall calls it the Night of Power. It has its own short surah, al-Qadr, five verses. It says this was the night the Qur'an was sent down, and then it asks: what will make you understand what the Night of Power is? And answers: "The Night of Power is better than a thousand months." The angels and the Spirit come down in it, by their Lord's permission, and it is peace until the rising of the dawn. So Muslims remember it as the night the revelation began, the night in the cave of Hira you met back in camp two. But which night is it? A hadith in Bukhari says seek it in the odd nights of the last ten. The twenty-first, twenty-third, twenty-fifth, twenty-seventh, twenty-ninth. Many communities give special weight to the twenty-seventh. And there's a story about why nobody knows for sure. In Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ came out one night to tell the people which night it was. On the way, he found two men quarreling. And the knowledge was taken up from him. He told them: perhaps that is better for you. So the not-knowing became part of the gift: people seek it on all ten. And Aisha once asked him: if I find it, what should I say? He taught her a short line, in Tirmidhi, that asks God, who loves to pardon, to pardon her. Not wealth. Not success. Pardon. On the night worth a lifetime, that was the request.
screen: `LAYLAT AL-QADR — POWER, MEASURE, DECREE.` · `BETTER THAN A THOUSAND MONTHS.` · `SEEK IT IN THE ODD NIGHTS.` · `TAKEN UP, BECAUSE OF A QUARREL.` · then, large: `ON THAT NIGHT, ASK FOR PARDON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one extra minute, every night. Tonight, before you sleep, add one minute of quiet you wouldn't have had. Sit up in bed, or on the floor, lights low. If you pray, pray a little more, or ask for pardon, the way Aisha was taught. If you don't, simply sit, and let it be a night you didn't let slip past. Then tomorrow night, do it again, and the next. You don't know which night matters most. That's the point. The bell holds the time.
Laylat al-Qadr. The Night of Power, when the Qur'an was first sent down, better than a thousand months, sought in the last ten nights. Today's word.
Your line: better than a thousand months. Tonight, treat one ordinary hour as if it might be the one that counts. Day one hundred twenty-four.

125.title: Ramadan: the fast of the tongue
125.hook: whoever doesn't leave false speech, Allah has no need of his hunger (Bukhari)
125.tomorrow: The charity of the fast's end
125.howItsDone: During Ramadan, Muslims try to fast from lying, gossip, arguing and harsh words as well as from food and drink, and many answer provocation with the words 'I am fasting'.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power. Your line was better than a thousand months. Did you treat one ordinary hour as if it might be the one? Day one hundred twenty-five.

It's four in the afternoon on a Ramadan day. No food since before dawn. No water. You're driving home, and someone cuts you off, hard, and then honks at you, as if it were your fault. Your hands tighten on the wheel. The words are right there, already in your mouth, and honestly, you've earned them. You're tired, you're hungry, and this person is wrong. Everything in you wants to roll down the window. The tradition has a sentence ready for this exact moment. Two words. Today: the fast of the tongue.
screen: `FOUR IN THE AFTERNOON, NO WATER.` → `SOMEONE CUTS YOU OFF.` → `THE WORDS ARE RIGHT THERE.`

segments.voice: Back on day eighteen, you heard a hadith from Bukhari about Ramadan. Here it is again, because this week it's the whole point: whoever does not give up false speech and acting on it, Allah has no need of their giving up food and drink. In other words, the stomach isn't the only thing that fasts. A fast with a sharp tongue has missed it. There's another report, in the Sunan of Ibn Majah, that's even blunter: many a person who fasts gets nothing from their fast except hunger. Just hunger. The whole day, and nothing to show but an empty stomach. So what do you do at four in the afternoon, when the words are right there? Another hadith in Bukhari answers it. It says fasting is a shield. And if someone fights with you or insults you while you're fasting, say: I am fasting. I am fasting. Twice. Not to them, necessarily. Maybe to yourself. It's a reminder of what you're doing today, and that what you're doing today is bigger than winning this moment. The word Ramadan, you'll remember, comes from a root for scorching heat. Some scholars have read that as the heat that burns away wrongdoing. Whether or not that's the origin, it's how many Muslims hear it. The month is meant to burn off more than a few pounds. Gossip. Lying. Complaining. The cutting remark. And the hope is that a month of holding the tongue leaves a habit behind, the way a month of early mornings does.
screen: `NO NEED OF THEIR HUNGER.` · `NOTHING BUT HUNGER.` · `SAY: I AM FASTING. TWICE.` · `A HEAT THAT BURNS AWAY WRONG.` · then, large: `THE TONGUE FASTS TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fast from one unkind word. Think of the person you're most likely to snap at today, or the conversation where your tongue tends to run. Picture it now, clearly: the tone, the moment, the words that usually come. Then picture yourself pausing, and saying, inside, I am fasting. Whether or not you're fasting from food, you can fast from that one word. Breathe out slowly. Let the picture end quietly. The bell holds the time.
Ramadan. The month of fasting, from a root for scorching heat; a fast of the tongue as well as the stomach. Today's word.
Your line: fast with the tongue too. When the sharp word comes today, say instead, even just to yourself: I am fasting. Day one hundred twenty-five.

126.title: The charity of the fast's end
126.hook: a small gift of food paid before the Eid prayer so the poor celebrate too
126.howItsDone: Before the Eid al-Fitr prayer, Muslim households give zakat al-fitr for every member, a measure of staple food or, in many communities, its cash value, usually through a mosque that passes it to people in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fast of the tongue, and the two words, I am fasting. Your line was fast with the tongue too. Did you catch one sharp word before it got out? Day one hundred twenty-six.

Look back at this week. A thread of moon low in the west. A meal in the dark before dawn. A date at sunset. Long nights of standing. A night worth a lifetime. A fast of the tongue. It's been a month in a week. And now it's almost over. Tomorrow is the feast. Somewhere tonight, a family is ironing new clothes and making sweets. And somewhere, not far away, a family is wondering what there'll be to eat tomorrow at all. Before the feast can start, the tradition asks for one thing. Today: the charity of the fast's end.
screen: `A MONTH IN A WEEK.` → `NEW CLOTHES, SWEETS.` → `AND A FAMILY WITH NOTHING.`

segments.voice: It's called zakat al-fitr, the charity of breaking the fast. A companion, Ibn Umar, describes it in Bukhari. The Prophet ﷺ made it obligatory: a sa' of dates or a sa' of barley, on every Muslim, free or enslaved, man or woman, young or old. And he ordered it to be paid before people go out to the Eid prayer. A sa' was a measure of volume, about four double handfuls: two cupped hands, filled, four times. Enough food for a family's day. Notice who it's on. Everyone. Not only the wealthy, like the yearly zakat you met in camp one. The head of a household pays for each person in it, even a baby born that month. Almost everyone gives; the poorest receive. Why? Another companion, Ibn Abbas, gives two reasons in the Sunan of Abu Dawud. It purifies the one who fasted from any idle or hurtful talk that slipped through the month; a kind of closing apology for yesterday's lesson. And it's food for the poor. Then he adds the timing: paid before the prayer, it's the zakat al-fitr. Paid after, it's just ordinary charity. The deadline is the point. The gift has to arrive in time for the poor to celebrate too, not the day after. Today most Muslims give its value, often through a mosque, which buys food or passes on the money. Schools differ on whether money counts or it must be food; the Hanafi school has long allowed money. But the aim hasn't changed in fourteen centuries. Nobody should be hungry on the feast.
screen: `A SA' OF DATES OR BARLEY.` · `ON EVERY MUSLIM, EVEN A BABY.` · `IT PURIFIES, AND IT FEEDS.` · `BEFORE THE PRAYER, NOT AFTER.` · then, large: `NOBODY HUNGRY ON THE FEAST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set aside a meal's worth. Cup your two hands together in front of you, as if holding grain. Fill them in your mind, four times: that's a sa'. Picture it as food on someone's table tomorrow. Then think of one real way you could give a meal's worth this week: a food bank, a neighbor, a coworker who's struggling, a mosque's collection. Decide on it now, before the moment passes. If you pray, you can ask that it reach someone in time. The bell holds the time.
Zakat al-fitr. The charity at the end of the fast: food given by nearly everyone, before the Eid prayer, so the poor celebrate too. Today's word.
Your line: everyone eats on eid. Before this week ends, give one meal's worth to someone who needs it, and give it in time. A week, done. Day one hundred twenty-six.
